author: Adnan
caption:
How does history gets turned into a story. Or maybe even HIS story?

You’ve got this huge Victorian monument( the William Wallace monument) , built more than 500 years after Wallace died, basically saying: this is who we think he was, and this is what we want him to represent.

Then Hollywood comes along and does the same thing.

Except now there’s blue face paint, kilts from the wrong century, no bridge in the Battle of Stirling Bridge, Andrew Moray pretty much disappears, and half the world walks away thinking they’ve learned Scottish history.

And that’s the bit I find fascinating.

Most people don’t remember the most accurate version of history. They remember the version that was told best.

Which is slightly terrifying when you think about it.

The girls and I talked about this while climbing the monument. Not just “what happened?”, but “who told us this happened?” and “what did they leave out?”

Because Braveheart is a great movie. I’m not trying to ruin anyone’s childhood here.

But it’s also a pretty good reminder that a compelling story can become more powerful than the truth underneath it.

And once that happens, correcting the story gets a lot harder.

#aazaadventures #WilliamWallace #ScottishHistory #Braveheart #Worldschooling

author: Adnan
caption:
Before most people could read, churches had already figured out visual storytelling.

Inside Saint Vincent in San Sebastián, the carvings, stained glass, figures and altarpiece weren’t simply there to make the building look impressive. They helped communicate stories, beliefs, power and morality to people who might never own a book.

In other words, this was mass media.

The difference is that nobody consumed it while half-watching, scrolling and checking notifications.

You had to stand there. Look closely. Notice the expressions, the gestures, the scale and the sequence.

And then step back.

That was the part I liked most. Up close, the church is hundreds of separate details. From the centre of the nave, it becomes one complete visual argument.

We often talk about art as something displayed inside buildings.

In Saint Vincent, the building is part of the artwork.

#aazaadventures

author: Adnan
caption:
There’s a tendency to walk into a cathedral like Saint-André, look up, say “wow,” take a few photos, and move on.

But buildings like this weren’t created just to impress people. They were designed to shape what people believed, who they obeyed, and how they understood their place in the world.

Exactly like Instagram, for those of you who partake.

Before mass literacy, television, or social media, architecture did a lot of the communicating. The scale told you who had power. 

The stained glass told stories. 

The sculptures taught lessons. 

Even the light was part of the message.
Hence all the stained glass.

And, of course, none of this appeared by magic. 

Generations of stonecutters, carpenters, artists, labourers and craftspeople spent their lives building something they would never see completed. 
Kings and bishops usually get remembered. 

The people carrying and placing the stone rarely do.

That’s what I find most interesting about places like the Cathédrale Saint-André de Bordeaux. 

It isn’t simply a beautiful old church. 
It’s a record of faith, politics, wealth, labour, ambition, destruction and repair, all occupying the same space.

History becomes much harder to simplify when you’re standing inside it.

#aazaadventures

caption:

The landscape felt different from a distance but surprisingly familiar up close. The views were vast fields of ferns, managed forests, and a few cow pastures. The vegetation was thick, the air humid, and tiny raindrops glistened on the leaves. Many of the plants reminded me of home. Wild blackberries were scattered along the trail, and Ayana and I sampled a few as we hiked. Afterward, we drove through the surrounding countryside with rolling hills and homes with traditional French tiled roofs.

author: Adnan
caption:
My daughters describe school as “six cruel hours of our lives.”

A little dramatic? Maybe.

Completely wrong? I’m not so sure.

Most education systems were designed for a world where information was scarce, adults controlled access to it, and everyone was expected to learn roughly the same thing, at roughly the same speed, while sitting in roughly the same chair.

That world no longer exists.

This year, we’re trying something different.

As we travel, the girls are writing blogs every day. They research the places we visit, follow questions that interest them, use voice-to-text to capture their thinking, and learn to use AI intentionally, responsibly, and ethically.

AI doesn’t do the thinking for them.

It helps them get started. Then they have to question the answers, verify the facts, decide what matters and add the observations that only they could have made.

That process requires judgment.

It requires curiosity, critical thinking, editing, communication, and the willingness to change your mind when the evidence doesn’t support your first idea.

In other words, many of the skills we keep saying education is supposed to teach.

They’re also working with the International Kids’ Council, created by our friends Jess and James Marsh alongside their son, Leo.

The IKC brings together young people from different countries to work on real problems, develop their own ideas, collaborate across cultures, and experience what it means for their voices to be taken seriously.

That matters.

Because children don’t suddenly become capable of contributing when they turn eighteen. They become capable by being trusted with meaningful work before then.

You can learn more about the International Kids’ Council here:

https://go.intl.education/ikc

I’m not claiming that travelling with your family is the answer for every child. It isn’t accessible to everyone, and worldschooling has its own costs, compromises, arguments, logistical disasters, and days when nobody feels particularly educational.

But I am questioning the limiting belief that meaningful learning must happen inside a classroom, according to someone else’s time.

#aazaadventures

author: Adnan
caption:
The cloister at Moissac is basically a medieval storybook carved into stone.

Around its walkways are 76 different capitals, filled with biblical scenes, saints, monsters, animals and plants. 

Not decoration for decoration’s sake. 

These images helped turn the cloister into a place of memory, teaching and reflection, at a time when books were scarce and literacy was far from universal.

What struck me was how much the sculptors managed to fit into such a small space. 

Characters bend around corners. 

Stories continue from one side of a capital to another. 

You have to walk around each pillar to understand what is happening.

Which feels deliberate.

The monks didn’t just look at these stories. 

They moved through them, day after day. 
History, belief and imagination built directly into their daily routine.

Nearly a thousand years later, I’m doing exactly what they intended: slowing down, circling the stone and trying to work out what the story is saying.

#aazaadventures #AbbayeDeMoissac #RomanesqueArt #MedievalHistory #Worldschooling

author: Adnan
caption:
Sunday morning at the Marché des Capucins.

Inside, Bordeaux was busy doing what Bordeaux does best: coffee, oysters, produce, conversation, and a fairly serious commitment to breakfast. (The bread is ridiculously yummy)

Outside the city, fires were spreading through Gironde.

That contrast stayed with me.

Markets make abundance look permanent. Rows of fruit. Fresh bread. Fish on ice. People choosing what to eat later, as if later is guaranteed.

Nothing is guaranteed. Except where we're all headed...

A short distance away (about 10km from.us) other people were watching alerts, packing cars, and waiting to see which way the wind would turn.

For a while, we were too as parts of Bordeaux were evacuated.

It didn’t make the market feel trivial. It made it feel fragile.

Ordinary life continues during a crisis.

And sometimes buying food, sharing a table, and keeping a city moving is part of how people hold things together.

Sometimes it just getting out there and saying bonjour to the people at the market.

Whatever works for you in that moment 

#aazaadventures

author: Adnan
caption:
Most cities have museums.

As does Toulouse but...

The streets are the museums here with statues  just scattered about.
I started noticing a pattern after a while. Statues weren't reserved for grand squares or government buildings. They appeared on fountains, around corners, attached to facades, tucked into small parks. 

Some celebrate military victories, others artists, writers, local heroes, or abstract ideas like the Republic itself.

Before photography, public sculpture was one of the ways a city decided what, and who, should be remembered.

It's like Instagram, but in real life, haha.

It made me wonder what we'd choose to build today. If anything... I do wonder how much we've lost because of ephemeral fleeting online posts. 

Like this one.

Maybe that's why I enjoy wandering cities like Toulouse. 

Every statue is a reminder that every generation leaves behind a story. The only question is whether the next generation will stop long enough to read it.

And that art takes time. To create. To make. To enjoy and relish.

author: Amy
caption:
We had a short stay in Bordeaux and luckily spent our first full day exploring parts of the old town. One highlight was climbing to the top of Basilica Saint-Michel’s bell tower, which stands separate from the Gothic church below. The 230-step spiral staircase led to a 360-degree view of Bordeaux. The top has wire surrounding the very narrow balcony with almost no openings for a camera lens until I realized I could crouch down and take photos through the flower-shaped cutouts.  Seeing Bordeaux from above helped us get our bearings and better understand the city. 

When we exited, the bells began to ring, and I suspect it would have been incredibly loud (photo 12 shows the bells). The Gothic church, largely built in the 15th century, has beautiful, intricate stained glass windows. 

Another highlight was the Miroir d’Eau, where a large plaza fills with a few inches of water. In 90-degree heat, we were all barefoot, sliding our feet through the water. Ayana wished she had brought her swimsuit—it was hard to walk around afterwards in wet clothes!

Bordeaux didn’t seem quite as beautiful to me as Toulouse. However, it did feel more diverse (though that may have been our neighborhood), with a large African diaspora, lots of barbershops, and great North African food. I may need to give Bordeaux another chance because we only had one full day of clear skies. The next two were filled with smoke and ash. Seeing the news that tens of thousands of people were being evacuated nearby made me realize just how extensive the fire was. We moved on to the southern coast, taking an alternate route because of the road closures. The last photo of the street art felt especially apropos as we walked through the city wearing our N95 masks.

author: Amy
caption:
We planned to go to Carcassonne by train from Toulouse, but we woke up to find that the afternoon return train had been cancelled due to the extreme heat. It was the second time we’d had a train cancelled because of the heat (the first was Marseille to Toulouse). We drove instead later in the week, and it worked out well to arrive early before the tour groups. We walked over the pedestrian bridge from the lower town. The medieval city rises out of the trees like a movie scene. We passed fresh-baked croissants and explored the outer walls before walking over the drawbridge. The city was waking up slowly, but once the crowds arrived, the place filled right up. We wandered the alleys and took in views from the city’s strategic hilltop location. This site has served as a fortified base for 2,500 years, beginning with the Romans. There was a small museum where the kids felt the heavy medieval armor, learned about the Black Death/bubonic plague, and finished with a competitive game of Carcassonne (the board game). We also found the best crepe-maker in France (best so far!), so we went back twice. Not only that, but his were half the price of elsewhere. Zarmina said it was a “great day” - a very high praise from this one! 😊

author: Adnan
caption:
One of the biggest misconceptions about Europe is that you have to visit museums to experience its history.

Sometimes you just walk into city hall.

Toulouse's Capitole has been the center of civic government for more than 800 years. Inside, the Salle des Illustres is filled with monumental paintings, gilded ceilings, chandeliers, and murals celebrating the city's history and identity.

What struck me wasn't just the craftsmanship. It was the fact that this isn't a preserved relic. People still come here to get married, city officials still work here, and decisions about Toulouse are still made within these walls.

That's something I keep noticing as I travel through France.

History isn't separated from everyday life. I mean, people live in Carcassonne!!

It's woven into it.

The places where people live, work, argue (we saw a couple arguing while we visited here!), celebrate, and govern are often the same places that house extraordinary works of art.

Maybe that's why these buildings feel so different. They're not monuments to the past. 

They're reminders that history is something we keep adding to.
📍 Capitole de Toulouse, France

author: Adnan
caption:
I climbed the 229 (girls think it was 230 but theyr incorrect, apparently) steps to the top of the Flèche Saint-Michel expecting the view to be the highlight.

And it was.

And also, it wasn't.

What I got.our of the experience was realizing that this tower wasn't originally attached to the basilica at all. Like many great bell towers in southwest France, it was built as a separate structure because the heavy vibrations from the bells could damage the church itself. 

And there are a LOT of bells in this tower!

The tower has also had a rough life. An earthquake in 1759 weakened its original spire, which was later dismantled for safety. The stone spire you see today is actually a 19th century reconstruction (reminiscent of the Carcassonne story), completed in 1869 during the restoration movement led by architect Paul Abadie.

Standing at the top, Bordeaux views in every direction. Medieval streets, grand boulevards, the Garonne River, and centuries of history... And the little people of course!

Also, notice the rooftop dinner tables??

Sometimes the best way to understand a place isn't by walking through it.

It's by climbing above it.

So, as many of my mentors have told me: go above and beyond.

author: Adnan
caption:
Carcassonne is not what you think. Well, it is certainly not what I thought at first glance. It's the kind of place that looks less believable the closer you get.

From the Pont Vieux, the towers seem almost too perfect, and unfortunately it is. 

The restoration of Carcassonne happened in the 19th century and it's the people who restored or who got to craft the story of what a mideval town/castle looked like. It's still.amazingly j lessive, just not "original". The person who we rented our car from (thank you Turo) is a history/french teacher r who clued me into this! Merci Johann!

But the part I loved wasn’t rushing through the gates. It was the approach, crossing the river, wandering the streets below, and watching the Cité keep appearing between rooftops and over stone walls.

Travel has a strange way of making the destination feel like the main event. Often, it’s the slow approach that gives a place its power. 

It's not about the end goal! Right folks?

Once I’m inside, Carcassonne becomes crowded streets, shops, restaurants, and people trying to photograph the same tower without getting seventeen strangers in the frame. (Guilty)

From outside, though, it still feels slightly... Mystical.

And sometimes the best view of a place comes before I’ve technically arrived.

#aazaadventures

author: Adnan
caption:
One thing about our recent adventures in France has completely ruined for me is the idea of a “quick stop.”

You walk into a church for five minutes, look up once, and suddenly you’re standing there studying centuries-old stained glass like you have nowhere else to be.

Basilique Saint-Michel sits in one of Bordeaux’s oldest neighborhoods, shaped by merchants, artisans, sailors, immigration, conflict, and constant reinvention. It feels less like a monument and more like a building that has absorbed whatever the city threw at it.

That is probably why I liked it.

The windows are beautiful, but not in a neat, untouched way. They carry damage, replacement, restoration, and changing taste. Some things survived because people valued them. Some disappeared because people didn’t.

Which is a slightly uncomfortable reminder that history is not only shaped by what happened.

It is shaped by what someone decided was worth keeping. And what was worth throwing away.... Sigh.

author: Amy
caption:
Toulouse surprised me with its beauty. All of these French cities seem to have a lovely old city center, but here it felt like the whole city was beautiful. It’s nicknamed La Ville Rose (“The Pink City”) because of the warm pink and terracotta bricks used throughout the city. I went out early one morning to take photos, and once the sunlight hit the brick buildings, they seemed to glow orange.

I wandered the streets and felt incredibly safe, even at 6:30 a.m. with my camera. There was a very large park (Jardin des Plantes) just half a block from our place. We visited it daily, enjoying its many benches, statues surrounded by lush flowers, shaded paths, and pedestrian bridges. If you read the kids’ blogs they really loved the Royal Garden section where there is a pond with ducks, ducklings, geese, bridges, and waterfalls. 

One day we painted in the park through a city-funded art program where anyone could stop by and try acrylic painting. We met a young Parisian woman whom Ayana quickly befriended. Another day, Ayana, Zarmina, and I brought our watercolors and painted together in the park. I’m a big fan of how the French use their public spaces. 

A church I had walked past that morning was one the kids wanted to explore later, Saint-Étienne Cathedral. It was awe-inspiring, with the stained glass casting rainbow-colored light across the floor and walls. I’m glad the kids recommended exploring it.

author: Adnan
caption:
Have you ever tames a monster? Or better yet, danced with one?

At @halledelamachine in Toulouse, the Minotaur doesn't just stomp across the stage. 

The minotaur Dances!

And then there's the woman, suspended high above him, floating, fearless, almost untouchable. Theovement is magical with her above and the minotaur below. (Neck did hurt watching the entire performance!)

It's a strange pairing. Beauty and brute force.
Control and surrender. 
Humanity and instinct.

Maybe that's the point.

Because that's what dance is all about. Challenging conceptions and preconceptions to get us to think through new possibilities where none may have existed before.

Capturing and releasing thoughts that are so fleeting you don't even know you're having them and then you realize, oh yes, I'm watching a performance. I'm not in it. This is not real. Or is it unreal?

We all carry a Minotaur inside us. Ego. Fear. Ambition. Rage. The parts we'd rather hide.or maybe I should say the parts I would hide, since this is my story... Then again, what's yours? 

What monsters lurk in your backyard? Don't tell me, show me. Or come visit Le Halle de la Machine in Toulouse. It's magical and the people (actors, scientists, dancers, performers) there are absolutely wonderful!

author: Amy
caption:
I found out the largest annual photo festival in the world was happening an hour away in Arles (Les Rencontres d’Arles). I decided to go solo because the kids can’t last in the intense heat and humidity and I wanted to see all that I could. The festival has over 30 exhibitions around the historic town and many inside the older buildings. It’s quite a contrast to see contemporary photography and anti-colonial themes inside of these ancient places. 

Not every exhibit was indoors — there was a “flower power” one that had large format photos around a park. I wandered past an amazing outdoor market with beautiful vintage items. I learned about Ghana’s history of fighting for freedom through photos, took a look at 200 years of animal photography and its themes, and checked out the photos from a scientist who gathers water samples around Marseille and figured out a way to make a gel and photograph the bacterial colors. I went by  the Van Gogh gardens and saw the Roman ruins that are right in the center of the old town. 

I am really glad I made the trip there but my drive home was stressful - I’ve now learned never to get below 100k gas in a car here because the gas stations are few and far between; my credit cards don’t work in the machines (I thankfully had euros); and there are nine types of gas and it’s not uncommon to have to go to another station to get the right gas the car needs. But I made it back with 2% on my phone and I’m here to write about it. 😬😊

author: Adnan
caption:
So many folks come to Marseille and go to the Old Port, the Fort Saint Jean, etc, but the actual substance, the heart of the city is up the hill in Le Panier.

It’s the oldest quarter, but it doesn't function like a static museum. It's an art gallery. The environment is entirely fluid. Local artists constantly paint over old murals, so the streets look different every few weeks.

We spent the morning navigating the alleys, checked out the 17th-century courtyard at La Vieille Charité, and stopped in a quiet square for some yummy treats.

Highly recommend getting here early in the morning. There was almost no one here at 7a on July 14th!

author: Amy
caption:
Le Panier district was a wonderful surprise. I spent time researching where to visit in Marseille and surrounding areas, but I hadn’t paid much attention to this neighborhood until the other day. There have been so many places to see and things to do.

I picked the right day to visit. We went very early (by French summer standards) and on a holiday. I hadn’t expected to find such elaborate street art, with virtually every corner displaying some kind of creativity. The streets have the classic look and charm of a historic French neighborhood, narrow alleyways, colorful shutters, stone buildings, and lanterns, but they’re also filled with graffiti, stickers, mosaics, shells, and other artistic details.

Le Panier is the oldest district in Marseille, built on the site of the city’s ancient Greek origins (I was surprised to learn it was a Greek settlement first). For much of the 20th century it was a rougher, less expensive neighborhood, which attracted artists and craftspeople. Over decades art became a part of the neighborhood and more recently it’s become a favorite area in Marseille. With few people around and shops closed, it was much easier to photograph. I wrote about it the other day but reliving some photos today. 

#aazatravels

author: Adnan
caption:
Most people think Fort Saint-Jean was built to protect Marseille.

Only half true.

Louis XIV also used it to keep watch over the city after Marseille dared to challenge the crown. Imagine building a fortress that's aimed as much at your own people as at invading armies... Fun times.

Today, it's one of the best places to wander in Marseille. Well, if it not so ridiculously hot. Like today. It's just a balmy warmish 80F // 25C. But somewhat rainy.

If you visit Marseille, don't just walk across the bridge to MuCEM. Slow down and explore the fort itself. 

But for now we're headed to the museum...

#aazaadventures

author: Amy
caption:
Aix-en-Provence is so beautiful. We arrived early-ish and walked the streets. Everything seems picturesque. The first stop was Pâtisserie Béchard for the decant treats. The large Saturday market was in full swing nearby. It’s a very popular town. Aix was built on top of water so there are many, supposedly, around 100 fountains around town. We saw one being used to cool some wine bottles. There is a well known fountain that looks like a bush with plants growing in it. There was a Harry Potter store tucked in an alleyway, much to Ayana’s delight. We ended our time in a bookstore/cafe browsing the books and eating lunch. It inspired the kids to request a lot more books for their kindles - sorry to the bookstore as we’re traveling pretty lightly. Honestly, I’d love to come back and spend more time here - with less people and a bit cooler! 

#aazatravels

I'll be sharing some more specific acts soon too.

author: Amy
caption:
YELLOW: We woke up early and roamed Le Panier district. It was surprisingly quiet until we confirmed with the one open coffee shop owner that it’s a holiday today. Tomorrow is the national holiday but perhaps people get both days off. Tonight there will be fireworks. It was so peaceful to walk the streets and check out the coolest street art area that I’ve seen, including alleys with actual art work hung up between beautiful green and flowering plants, decorated doors, and decorative fabrics hung where people have made a wish. I’ll be back to this area. Note that not all photos are from Le Panier but the majority. Can you see Adnan? 

#aazatravels

author: Amy
caption:
Calanques: The three hour boat ride along the Calanques National Park is really pretty and even reminded me of a boat ride we took in the Algarve region in Portugal. We went from Marseille to Cassis and back. The guide said the city has been here for 2,600 years (obviously not including the time before when the Casquer caves were used up to 33,000 year ago!). I was glad to take the early 9:30am tour because the weather was so hot, even with the boat moving and creating some wind. The captain drove the boat into one of the narrow limestone crevasses which was slightly alarming as the waves pushed us forward into a space too tight for the boat (photos 9 and 10). The scale of the cliffs is hard to capture. I’m glad we did the boat ride despite questioning the decision to do so the day before! Admittedly, a few of us felt a little sea sick part of the time. 

#aazatravels

author: Amy
caption:
RED: I picked red as soon as I saw the cute house with red and the red gate. Today we went to La Ciotot, about a 30 mins drive from where we are staying.  We started at the Park du Mugel and hopped in the water at the small pebbly beach. I walked around the botanical garden where the crickets make a strong buzzing sound. Sunday is the big market day with food and products. We had a tasty lunch at La Petite Creperie. We learned that most places finish up breakfast at 11am and close until noon for lunch. We happened to be looking at 11am! We met up with Rachel, who knew the assignment (red shirt!). 😁 Ayana took that photo 🙏.

author: Amy
caption:
This church, Notre Dame de la Guarde, sits at the top of Marseille and “watches over the city and its sailors.” There are strings of model boats hanging from the ceiling which have come from sailors grateful to the Virgin Mary for saving them from shipwrecks and storms. The outside of the church looks pretty but the inside was surprisingly bright and gold. The entire floor is covered in small mosaic stones. We took a little tourist train car up to the top but I was very impressed seeing people walking up to this place in midday humid heat. We walked down and even that was almost too hot! There is a view of all of Marseille from here. 

#aazatravels

author: Amy
caption:
I had every intention to go to the Mucem, the well known museum right along the water. I walked towards the building and saw a bright kiosk “Les Billets” tickets! And purchased three for me and the kids. As we walked inside, I realized that I’m at a completely different museum! It was a “happy accident” as Adnan said. It was the Cosquer Caves, which took us to a life size replica of these caves that were discovered by Henri Cosquer in the 80’s by scuba diving. With zero expectations, we ended up having a great time. We learned a lot about these caves and the kids were really inspired by the experiential nature of the cave “ride” (like a Disney ride) that moved us past the stalagmites and chandelier formations and pointed out all the cool paintings and hand prints in the cave. These date back as far as 33,000 years ago! The glaciers held so much water back then that the caves were accessible for humans to walk into them. The water levels were 400 feet lower. The paintings show lots of extinct animals like the Megaloceros (Ayana’s standing under one). The cave wasn’t lived in but perhaps seen as a spiritual place. Post ride we saw the life sized animal replicas. There’s also a message about climate change - there was little change in our ocean levels for 6000 but that’s going to change rapidly as the glaciers begin to melt. The more the water levels rise, these paintings will be destroyed. 

We did meander over to the Mucem but the exhibits were going to be too much for one day. We instead walked through the cool building and over to the fort and jardin and then to a pedestrian bridge to a nice area for lunch. It was the hottest day yet so we’re kind of melting when a guy offered to take a photo of the three of us. 

#aazatravels

author: Amy
caption:
We’re staying in Vallon des Auffes area in Marseille. It’s a little outside the city center but it’s very beautiful. It has a good energy. We took an evening walk and the warm light at sunset was so beautiful. The people on the rocks remind me of what would be seals in San Francisco! Evening walks along the main road feel a bit chaotic with cars, bikers, and the many runners dodging around us. 

#aazatravels

author: Amy
caption:
Cassis is a very cute town about 45 mins from Marseille. I heard a lot of English spoken, ie it’s popular with the tourists. I can see why. It has that quintessential French Rivera vibe. A million ice cream shops beckoning on every corner. There is a beach in the center of town with a literal sea of humanity. So many people on holiday on the sand and in the sea. We rented an umbrella and chairs - pricey but worth it - as the sand is a mix of pebbles, shale and sand. The water is refreshing albeit a touch unclean at the shore. I’d love to come back and explore more. Nearby is Calanques National park and there are beautiful limestone cliffs in the area. It felt a bit like stepping into a postcard. 

#aazatravels

author: Adnan
caption:
Paris has the Louvre, the Eiffel Tower, Notre Dame.... and then it's got....
The Marché aux Puces, where every object looks like it has seen seven lifetimes worth of events and is currently judging your clothing choices. I definitely felt judged.

Old signs, strange lamps, velvet chairs, cracked mirrors, toys from my childhood (just mine), vintage clothing (like REAL vintage), impossible chandeliers, and the occasional thing you’re not sure is art, plumbing, or could it be used as evidence in a court case?

This is my kind of place to hang, if it weren't so dang HOT! Well, it'll cool down. Eventually.... LeBigSigh.

#aazaadventures

author: Amy
caption:
Zarmina’s main goal this year is exploring/tasting different foods. She’s got a sweet tooth so it leans heavily towards dessert. We’ve had some tasty food so far. The chocolate mousse (in Paris) doesn’t look amazing but it was incredible. The pizza is from a local restaurant near our place and I hope to go back. It opened for dinner at 7pm and we luckily arrived soon after as it filled right up. Marseille is very crowded this time of year (as expected). I didn’t realize until later Ayana made her own mustache with ice cream. 

#aazatravels

I’m very impressed she came to France speaking neither French or English but now is fluent in both after four years. I found her class on Airbnb experiences. I hope to paint more as we move around, and this class inspired me.

author: Amy
caption:
One weekday around lunch, we walked to a nearby park that was bustling with hundreds of people out and about - eating lunch in pairs on park benches, huddled in friend groups on picnic blankets, leisurely walking their dogs with friends, and enjoying the pleasant weather outside. We sat and observed while I had honey bees flying around in the wildflowers behind me. It was so great to see a beautiful park so well loved. 

#aazatravels

author: Amy
caption:
I loved Musée d’Orsay and the Renoir exhibit (maybe took too many photos of paintings!). I bought the kids audio guides and then had some FOMO and got one for myself. It made it much easier to absorb the information on so many paintings. The Renoir theme was about love and connections, and there were several paintings with women that could have been a celebration of same sex relationships (ahead of his time in the mid 1800’s). He also “eliminated gender domination” and showed happy bonds between men and women.

The Musée d’Orsay building is a piece of art itself as a former train station. The museum was created to bridge the gap between the older art at the Louvre and the modern art at the Pompidou Centre, showcasing the impressionist era. The view from the 5th floor is really stunning and looked absolutely surreal!

#aazatravels

author: Amy
caption:
The Arc de Triomphe, built over 30 years in the early 1800’s, is very impressive. Napoleon wanted it built to honor the French fighters post-Battle of Austerlitz, but he didn’t get to see it completed. His casket did ride through the Arc after it was completed. The eternal burning fire is checked on daily by the military to be rekindled. The roundabout is a bit chaotic. I’m thankful to not be driving here!

#aazatravels

There will be some online math, reading (because they love to), and writing (to record our travels and to share stories with our friends). We know that so much learning happens through experiences. We (the parents) will be learning along with the kids too.
